transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

Given that you’ve already ruled out the most common issues (filter and blockages), and considering the specific symptom of cutting out after 5–10 seconds on an older unit, this is highly characteristic of a battery degradation issue or a thermal protection trigger.

Here’s a breakdown of what’s likely happening and how to troubleshoot it:

### 1. The Battery (Most Likely Culprit)
At 5 years old, the lithium-ion battery in your Dyson V-series model is well past its optimal lifespan (typically 3–4 years with regular use).
• Why it cuts out: As batteries age, their internal resistance increases and voltage drops under load. When you start the vacuum, the motor draws high current. If the battery can’t sustain that voltage for more than a few seconds, the system interprets this as a fault or low power and shuts down to protect itself.
• The "intermittent" nature: This explains why it works some days but not others. Temperature affects battery chemistry (cold = worse performance), and slight variations in how deeply discharged it was before charging can change whether it survives the initial high-draw startup phase.
• Test: Try running it on the lowest power setting ("Eco"). If it runs for longer than 10 seconds, but still cuts out eventually or when you switch to higher modes, this strongly points to battery failure.

### 2. Thermal Protection (Overheating)
Dyson vacuums have a thermal cut-off sensor. If the motor gets too hot, it shuts down and won’t restart for ~30–60 minutes.
• Why it cuts out early: If the airflow is restricted even slightly (e.g., a clogged pre-motor filter that isn’t visibly dirty but is saturated with fine dust, or a partially blocked cyclone), the motor overheats rapidly. After 5–10 seconds of high load, it trips.
• Check: Feel the body of the vacuum near the motor housing (usually where the battery attaches) after it cuts out. If it’s very hot to the touch, this is likely an airflow/overheating issue, not just a battery one.

### 3. Battery Contact Issue
Since it’s intermittent, check for poor electrical connection between the battery and the vacuum body.
• Test: Remove the battery, inspect the metal contacts on both the battery and the vacuum for corrosion or debris. Clean them with a dry cloth (or isopropyl alcohol if corroded). Reinsert firmly. Sometimes wiggling the battery slightly while it’s running can tell you if it’s a loose contact issue.

### 4. Motor Fault (Less Likely but Possible)
If the motor brushes are worn out (in models that have them), they may cause intermittent sparking and shutdowns. However, Dyson V-series models typically use brushless motors, which don’t wear in this way. This is less common than battery failure at the 5-year mark.

---

### Recommended Next Steps:
1.  Perform a "Low Power" Test: Run it on Eco mode. If it lasts longer but still fails under higher load, replace the battery.
2.  Check for Heat: After a shutdown, feel if the unit is overheating. If yes, try replacing the filter again (even if clean) or ensure no hidden blockages exist in the wand/hose connections.
3.  Reset the Vacuum: Unplug the charger and remove the battery. Hold the power button for 30 seconds to drain residual charge. Reattach battery and charger, then try again. This can sometimes reset the battery management system.
4.  Replace the Battery: Given the age (5 years) and symptoms, this is the most probable fix. Dyson batteries are replaceable. You can buy an official replacement or a reputable third-party one. Note: Third-party batteries vary in quality; official ones ensure compatibility with the safety systems.

Bottom Line: With a 5-year-old V-series Dyson that passes basic cleaning checks, battery failure is the #1 suspect. The intermittent nature and short runtime under load are classic signs of aged cells unable to handle peak current draw.

Ok. On Max it nearly always stops within a few seconds, and it's less often on the lower setting. Battery isn't swollen or hot. It's been left on the charger permanently, if that matters. Is that enough to say it's the battery before I spend £60+?

Based on those details, yes, it is almost certainly the battery.

Here’s why:

1.  "Max" cuts out in seconds: This is the classic symptom of a battery that can no longer deliver the high current (amperage) required by the motor under load. The voltage sags immediately, and the computer shuts the vacuum down to protect itself.
2.  Lower settings work better: On Eco or Auto mode, the power draw is much lower. A degraded battery might still be able to handle this light load for a while, which explains why it works "sometimes" on lower settings but fails instantly on Max.
3.  Age (5 years): Lithium-ion batteries in cordless vacuums typically last 3–4 years with regular use. At 5 years, capacity and internal resistance are often severely degraded.
4.  Left on charger permanently: While modern Dysons have charging circuits that prevent overcharging, keeping a lithium battery at 100% charge continuously (especially in a warm environment like a garage or utility room) accelerates chemical aging. It’s likely the cells are "starved" of capacity due to long-term high-voltage stress.

### Is it worth spending £60+?
That depends on the model and your expectations:

• If you have a V8, V10, or V11: A new battery is often 30–50% of the cost of a refurbished unit. If you’re only getting ~5 minutes on Max anyway (which is standard for old batteries), ask yourself if it’s worth £60+ to get that back for another year or two. Many people find it more economical to save toward a newer model with better battery tech.
• If you have a V12, V15, or V20: These are more expensive machines. A new battery (£80–£100) might be worth it if you rely heavily on the high-power settings for deep cleaning.

### Before you buy: Try this "Reset"
Sometimes, the battery management system gets confused. Try this once before spending money:
1.  Remove the battery from the vacuum and the charger.
2.  Leave both out of the machine for at least 30 minutes (this allows residual charge to drain).
3.  Reattach the battery to the charger only (not the vacuum) and let it charge fully (usually 4.5 hours).
4.  Try using it on Max immediately after charging.

If it still cuts out in seconds, the battery is dead. You’ll need a replacement or a new vacuum.
